prompt: Which part of lesson 1's planner does a meta-framework's router replace?

choices.text: The `page` function that chose a page from the address
choices.why: Right. A router does the same, filled in from files or a list.

choices.text: The `esc` function
choices.why: Escaping is still done, by the framework's templates, but it is not routing.

choices.text: `courses.json`
choices.why: The data stays; all four projects read the same file.

choices.text: The stylesheet
choices.why: Styles have nothing to do with which page an address shows.

prompt: What is a loader, in the sense this lesson uses?

choices.text: A progress spinner the framework shows while a slow page is still loading
choices.why: That is a loading indicator, not the loader the table names.

choices.text: A server function per route, its result sent with the page
choices.why: Yes. SvelteKit's load is the plainest example of it.

choices.text: The bundler that turns TypeScript into JavaScript
choices.why: That is the build, a different row of the table.

choices.text: The browser's module loader
choices.why: The browser loads scripts either way; a loader runs on the server.

prompt: Which cost of a meta-framework does building every page ahead of time remove?

choices.text: The JavaScript sent to the browser
choices.why: A prerendered page still ships the framework and hydrates.

choices.text: Learning where each file of the project runs
choices.why: The rules are the same whether a page is built ahead or not.

choices.text: A Node server that has to stay up
choices.why: Right. Files can be handed out by any static host.

choices.text: Changes between major versions
choices.why: A major version can change a static site's build as much as a server's.

prompt: Why does this lesson use Angular 21 and not 22?

choices.text: Angular 22 dropped server rendering from its CLI
choices.why: It has; the lesson says everything shown works the same in 22.

choices.text: Angular 22's CLI refuses Node 22.22.0
choices.why: Yes. It asks for 22.22.3 or later, and the track installs only one Node.

choices.text: Angular 21 is the newest one
choices.why: 22 is newer; the capture shows its CLI refusing.

choices.text: Angular 22 needs an npm newer than the one Node 22 ships
choices.why: The refusal names a Node version, not an npm one.

prompt: `npm install` in the Angular project stops with `Cannot read properties of null (reading 'edgesOut')`. What does the lesson do about it?
hint: The bug is in how npm resolves one kind of dependency.

choices.text: Installs a newer npm for the whole computer
choices.why: The course keeps the npm that came with Node.

choices.text: Deletes package-lock.json and node_modules and runs the install again
choices.why: There was no lockfile yet; the CLI skipped the install.

choices.text: Sets legacy-peer-deps in its .npmrc
choices.why: Right. npm then installs what package.json lists and leaves peer dependencies alone.

choices.text: Switches the project to Angular 22
choices.why: Angular 22 refuses this Node, which is why the lesson uses 21.

prompt: What does `pin.mjs` read to learn the version npm installed?

choices.text: `package-lock.json`
choices.why: Yes. The lockfile records the exact version of every package installed.

choices.text: The npm registry, over the network
choices.why: It never makes a request; it reads two local files.

choices.text: Each package's README
choices.why: A README has no reliable version in it.

choices.text: The ranges already written in package.json
choices.why: A range says which versions are allowed, not which one was installed.

prompt: Which of the four does not use file-based routing?

choices.text: Next.js
choices.why: Its routes are folders under app/.

choices.text: Nuxt
choices.why: Its routes are files under app/pages/.

choices.text: SvelteKit
choices.why: Its routes are folders under src/routes/.

choices.text: Angular
choices.why: Right. It declares routes in a list in app.routes.ts.

prompt: Match each framework to the file that answers `/courses/git`.
In a file-based router, you save a page as `app/course/[slug]/page.tsx` instead of `app/courses/...`. What happens?
hint: A file in the wrong folder is not an error.

choices.text: The build stops with a message naming the folder that has no matching route
choices.why: That is how a list of routes fails, not a folder of them.

choices.text: Only the singular address works
choices.why: Yes. The folder is the address, so a different folder is a different address.

choices.text: The framework corrects the name to the closest route
choices.why: No router guesses what an address should have been.

choices.text: Both addresses work
choices.why: Only the folder that exists is a route.

prompt: In the Next.js project, why were the course pages rendered at build time with no line asking for it?

choices.text: Every App Router page is static in Next.js 16
choices.why: A page that reads uncached data or a request API is rendered per request.

choices.text: `next start` renders every page once when it starts, before taking requests
choices.why: The route table was printed by the build, before any server ran.

choices.text: Their data is cached and their slugs are listed
choices.why: Right. Under Cache Components, cached data plus known parameters means a page can be built once.

choices.text: The project has no server components
choices.why: Every component in it is a server component.

prompt: In the build's route table, what does `◐` beside `/courses/[slug]` mean?

choices.text: The route failed to build
choices.why: A failure stops the build; the table is printed when it succeeds.

choices.text: A shell for unlisted slugs, filled on request
choices.why: Yes. The legend calls it a partial prerender, with content streamed by the server.

choices.text: The page is rendered only in the browser
choices.why: The legend says prerendered as static HTML, with server-streamed content.

choices.text: The three listed courses are out of date
choices.why: They are marked ○, built at build time.

prompt: In Next.js, a component in `app/` runs on the server unless its file starts with the directive `"use ___"`.
hint: The other side of the conversation.

prompt: Where does the Nuxt project read `courses.json`?

choices.text: In `server/api/plan.get.ts`
choices.why: Right. The pages ask for /api/plan with useFetch.

choices.text: In `nuxt.config.ts`
choices.why: The configuration sets the title and language, not the data.

choices.text: In `app/app.vue`
choices.why: That file only places <NuxtPage /> inside <main>.

choices.text: In the browser, from `public/`, as the plain planner does
choices.why: The file sits in the project's folder, read by the server.

prompt: During a server render, what does `useFetch("/api/plan")` do differently from the browser?

choices.text: Nothing: both make the same HTTP request
choices.why: On the server it calls the endpoint without going over the network.

choices.text: It calls it directly and sends the result in the page
choices.why: Yes. In the browser it then finds the result there and does not fetch again.

choices.text: It skips the data, and the browser fetches it after hydration
choices.why: The page arrived with the sessions in it, so the server had the data.

choices.text: It reads the data from the build
choices.why: Nothing was rendered at build time; the server reads the file on request.

prompt: You copy only `.output/` to another computer with Node 22 and run `node .output/server/index.mjs`. What happens?

choices.text: It fails: the project's 200 MB of node_modules are missing
choices.why: The built server carries its own small node_modules.

choices.text: It starts, but every page falls back to being rendered in the browser
choices.why: The server renders exactly as it did on the first computer.

choices.text: It serves the app, if courses.json is beside it
choices.why: Right. The packages travel with it; the data file is read from the working folder.

choices.text: It rebuilds the app first
choices.why: index.mjs starts a server; it never builds.

prompt: In SvelteKit, which file holds code that runs only on the server?

choices.text: `+page.svelte`
choices.why: The component runs on the server and again in the browser.

choices.text: `+page.server.ts`
choices.why: Yes. Its load runs only on the server, and its result becomes the page's data.

choices.text: `vite.config.ts`
choices.why: It configures the build; it is not part of a route.

choices.text: `src/app.html`
choices.why: That is the page template around every route.

prompt: A tutorial imports `$lib/plan`. What does SvelteKit 3's build do?

choices.text: Refuses it and names `#lib`
choices.why: Right. $lib was removed, and the error says how to keep it if you want to.

choices.text: Accepts it silently, as an alias of `#lib`
choices.why: The capture shows a build failure naming module_removed_lib.

choices.text: Builds, and the page fails in the browser
choices.why: It never gets that far; the build stops.

choices.text: Downloads `$lib` from npm
choices.why: $lib was never a package; it was an alias for src/lib.

prompt: What does SvelteKit's adapter decide?

choices.text: Which UI framework the project uses
choices.why: That is Svelte, whatever the adapter.

choices.text: How pages are routed, and which folder holds the routes
choices.why: Routing comes from src/routes/ and does not change with the adapter.

choices.text: What the build turns the app into
choices.why: Yes. Another adapter would produce static files, or a package for a host.

choices.text: Whether TypeScript is checked
choices.why: npm run check does that, whatever the adapter.

prompt: Angular's server answered `/courses/git` with an empty `<app-root>`. Why?

choices.text: The component threw while rendering
choices.why: The log names the Host header, not an error in a component.

choices.text: courses.json was missing from public/
choices.why: The file was there; the server never got as far as fetching it.

choices.text: localhost was not an allowed host
choices.why: Right. Naming the host with ng config and building again fixed it.

choices.text: RenderMode.Server sends an empty page by design and fills it in the browser
choices.why: RenderMode.Server renders on each request; RenderMode.Client is the empty one.

prompt: Why is an Angular server that fetches its own data over HTTP exposed to server-side request forgery if it trusts any Host header?

choices.text: Because HTTP is not encrypted between the server and itself
choices.why: Encryption is not the issue; the destination is.

choices.text: Its relative URLs are resolved against that header
choices.why: Yes. The server would make that call with its own network access, which is the danger.

choices.text: Because a browser that sends a forged Host can read the server's memory
choices.why: No browser can; the risk is the request the server makes.

choices.text: Because TransferState sends the data to every host
choices.why: TransferState only carries data into the page being rendered.

prompt: After `ng config` and a new build, how many static routes did Angular prerender?
Why does `tools/weigh.ts` count JavaScript before compression?

choices.text: Compressed sizes cannot be measured in Chromium
choices.why: They can; the first version of a tool like this would measure them.

choices.text: The servers compress differently
choices.why: Right. SvelteKit's adapter precompressed its files and Angular's Express server compressed nothing.

choices.text: Compression makes JavaScript run faster
choices.why: The browser decompresses before running; the code is the same.

choices.text: Browsers do not accept compressed scripts
choices.why: They do, and most servers send them.

prompt: How many of the five servers answered `/courses/nonsense` with a 404?
Next.js called `notFound()` and the response was still 200. What is the reason?

choices.text: The status went out with the shell
choices.why: Yes. A status cannot change once a response has started; lesson 4 is about that.

choices.text: `notFound()` only works in development
choices.why: It worked: the not-found page and the noindex tag were streamed into the response.

choices.text: `next start` ignores status codes
choices.why: It sends them; this one was sent before it was known.

choices.text: The page forgot to check for a missing course
choices.why: It checked and called notFound(), which is why the 404 page was in the body.

prompt: Why does a server-rendered page that hydrates carry its data inside a `<script>`?

choices.text: So the script need not fetch it again
choices.why: Right. The HTML alone is not enough to rebuild the page from.

choices.text: So search engines can read it
choices.why: Search engines read the HTML; the data is for the script.

choices.text: Because HTML cannot contain numbers
choices.why: The HTML shows the minutes perfectly well.

choices.text: To keep it hidden from the person reading the page, who sees only the HTML
choices.why: Anything in the page can be read by whoever has it.

prompt: Which of these servers put the titles of the two other courses into the Git page? Choose all that apply.
hint: Read the last column of payload.ts.

choices.text: Nuxt
choices.why: Yes: useFetch recorded the whole response of /api/plan.

choices.text: Angular
choices.why: Yes: TransferState recorded the whole courses.json.

choices.text: SvelteKit
choices.why: Its load returned one course only.

choices.text: Next.js
choices.why: It sent the rendered tree, which shows one course.

choices.text: lesson 1's server.ts
choices.why: It wrote no inline script at all.

prompt: A server component reads an API key from the environment to call another service. What reaches the browser?

choices.text: The key, inside the self.__next_f payload
choices.why: The payload holds the rendered tree, not the values the component read.

choices.text: Only what the component rendered from the result
choices.why: Yes. Data a server component reads stays on the server unless it is rendered.

choices.text: The key and the result, both serialised
choices.why: Neither is sent unless an element shows it.

choices.text: Nothing: server components send no HTML
choices.why: They send their HTML; what they do not send is their code.

prompt: In which of the four does a page's rendering follow from what its code reads, with no setting?

choices.text: Nuxt
choices.why: Nuxt decides in routeRules, in one file.

choices.text: Next.js
choices.why: Right. Cached reads make a page static; request APIs make it dynamic.

choices.text: SvelteKit
choices.why: SvelteKit uses an export beside load.

choices.text: Angular
choices.why: Angular uses RenderMode in app.routes.server.ts.

prompt: Match each line to what it makes a SvelteKit route do.

pairs.right: Built at build time into a file
Left to the browser to render
Sent with no JavaScript at all

prompt: A route is prerendered. Which of these is still true of it?

choices.text: It sends no JavaScript
choices.why: It still ships the framework and hydrates, unless the page drops it, as csr = false does.

choices.text: It is rendered again on every request
choices.why: That is the other mode; prerendered means once, at build time.

choices.text: It needs a Node server to be served
choices.why: A prerendered page is a file any static host can serve.

choices.text: It still hydrates
choices.why: Yes. Only the moment the HTML was made has moved.

prompt: A Vue team wants server rendering. Which choice does the lesson call almost always right?

choices.text: Nuxt, Vue's own
choices.why: Right. Switching framework to get another meta-framework rewrites every component.

choices.text: SvelteKit, because it ran the least JavaScript
choices.why: Moving to Svelte means rewriting every Vue component.

choices.text: Next.js, because it is the most widely used of the four
choices.why: Next.js is React's; it would mean leaving Vue.

choices.text: None: lesson 1's server.ts is enough for everyone
choices.why: It stops being enough at a size the lesson describes.

prompt: Which of these is a sign that the plain app has outgrown itself?

choices.text: It has a stylesheet
choices.why: Every app has one.

choices.text: Its forms must work without the script
choices.why: Yes. Handling posts on the server as well is what the frameworks already do.

choices.text: It is written in TypeScript and checked by tsc
choices.why: The plain planner already is.

choices.text: It reads a JSON file
choices.why: The plain planner does that in two places.

prompt: Put in order what happens to a request for `/courses/git` on the Nuxt server.
items: The page is rendered to HTML
The browser hydrates without fetching again

prompt: Match each meta-framework to the place where it decides a route's rendering.

pairs.right: An export beside the route's load
